newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Ignoring China anger, US envoy sees Taiwan leader.
newsitem.headline: Ignoring China anger, US envoy sees Taiwan leader.

text.p: U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers met with Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui on Tuesday in the most senior U.S.-Taiwan contact in nearly two years -- and one certain to anger China.
"President Lee thanked Deputy Treasury Secretary Summers for the United States' supoprt for our bid to join the World Trade Organisation," the presidential office said in a statement.
The meeting was the most senior U.S.-Taiwan contact since a visit to the Nationalist-ruled island by U.S. Transportation Secretary Federico Pena in December 1994.
"Summers affirmed the substantial meaning of the vice minister economic dialogue, which has increased bilateral economic and trade relations," the statement said.
Taiwan and Washington, which do not have diplomatic ties, agreed to hold three annual economic dialogues at the vice ministerial level starting from 1995.
The agreement was reached after the Clinton administration adjusted U.S. policy toward Taiwan in 1994 to strengthen bilateral economic ties.

The Lee-Summers talks came more than a year after Lee's visit to the United States in June 1995, an ostensibly private trip that included no known meetings with U.S. officials but which nonetheless outraged China.
China, Taiwan's rival since a civil war split them in 1949, indicated last week it would be unhappy if Summers visited Taiwan and held high-level meetings with Taiwanese officials.
Summers on Monday acknowledged discussing trade and other bilateral issues in meetings with economics Vice Minister Hsu Ke-sheng and other financial and foreign affairs officials.

In a news conference after those meetings, Summers would not comment on the political sensitivities surrounding his visit to Taiwan, which China regards as a rebel province ineligible for sovereign contacts with foreign governments.
He said such meetings would continue into the "indefinite future" as a matter of U.S. policy.
Summers hailed the island's powerhouse economy and urged it to play a wider international role in Asia, saying he looked forward to Taiwan's entry to the World Trade Organisation.

China reacted angrily to Lee's U.S. visit, saying it showed that Taiwan wanted independence rather than reunification with the mainland and that Washington, which switched ties to Beijing from Taipei in 1979, was colluding in the scheme.

Beijing responded by downgrading its U.S. ties, suspending semi-official talks with Taipei and launching nine months of war games and missile tests in waters near Taiwan in what it said was intended to thwart Taiwan's independence bid.
China says it will retake Taiwan by force if it tries to gain independence.
Taiwan is recognised by only 30 countries but uses its economic strength to keep close business ties with many of China's diplomatic partners.
In early September, a high-profile delegation led by John Anderson, Australia's minister for primary industries and energy, visited Taiwan for a three-day business forum.
Anderson vowed to strengthen economic ties with Taiwan despite repeated protests from China, which called Anderson's visit "unacceptable."
